title: In every heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaakur, and your line: lord of all. Did an insect get a ride outside instead of a paper towel? Yesterday the circle widened to every living thing. Today it moves inward, to the heart. Day five hundred twenty-three.

A subway car at rush hour. Forty strangers, shoulder to shoulder, all carefully not looking at one another. A man in a suit reading his phone. A teenager with headphones and eyes closed. A grandmother with grocery bags, a nurse just off a night shift. Each face closed, like a house with the curtains drawn. You could ride with them every day for a year and never know one name. The twenty-second ashtpadi makes a claim about every one of those closed houses. Someone lives inside.
screen: `FORTY STRANGERS, NOT LOOKING.` → `EACH FACE A CLOSED HOUSE.` → `SOMEONE LIVES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the One is spread through all beings. The twenty-second ashtpadi presses the point home: God dwells in every heart, ghat ghat, in each body and each being. Ghat literally means a pot or vessel, a clay jar. Gurbani uses it for the body, and for the heart inside it, the way a jar holds water. Ghat ghat, doubled, means in every single one. Gurbani returns to this again and again. In Sohila, the prayer before sleep, Guru Nanak sings, in paraphrase: within all is the Light, and You are that Light; by its shining, everything shines. Every face on that subway car is a clay jar with the same Light inside. This is the ground under some very practical things Sikhs do. It's why the langar, the free kitchen, seats everyone on the floor in the same rows, whoever they are. It's why the Gurus spoke so sharply against treating people as high or low by caste. And it's why, for Sikhs, seva, serving others, is never only charity. If the Light is in every heart, then serving a stranger is serving the One who lives there. That's a demanding teaching. It's easy to see the Light in a smiling child, or a kind friend. It's harder in the man who shoved past you to get a seat. Sukhmani doesn't make an exception for him. Ghat ghat means every jar.
screen: `GHAT GHAT: IN EVERY VESSEL.` · `THE SAME LIGHT IN EACH.` · `THE GROUND UNDER LANGAR AND SEVA.` · `NO EXCEPTIONS, EVEN THE RUDE ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for Him in one face. Bring to mind one face, or look at one, a photo or a person nearby. Choose someone ordinary, not your favorite person in the world. Look slowly: the eyes, the lines, the expression. Then hold the thought: there's Light in this jar too. Stay with it as long as you can. If it feels easy, choose a harder face. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you look. The bell holds the time.
Ghat ghat, in every vessel: Sukhmani says God dwells in every vessel, every body and heart, and Sohila adds that the same Light shines in all.
Your line: every heart. Today, look one stranger in the eye, a cashier, a driver, someone on the street, and offer a real hello. Day five hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that God dwells ghat ghat, in every heart, a teaching lived out in langar's shared rows and in seva to all.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ghat ghat, in every vessel; ghat is a clay jar, used for the body and heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: in every heart is a sweet saying about love.
what it means: God's Light lives in every body and heart, including the hard ones, so serving anyone is serving God.
what a scholar hears: ghat, a clay water jar, is a recurring Gurbani image for the body, and underlies the Gurus' rejection of high and low by caste.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Sohila was called 'the evening prayer', which clashes with day 524 (Rehras is the evening prayer); now 'the prayer before sleep'. Removed the superlative 'some of the most practical things'.
The outline places 'He dwells in every heart' in ashtpadi 22; the writer did not pin the exact line and paraphrased the theme with ghat ghat. A Keeper should identify the stanza.
Sohila paraphrase (sabh meh jot jot hai soe; tis dai chaanan sabh meh chaanan hoe), Ang 13: confirm.
